meta.title: Body Fluids
meta.summary: You are, more than anything else, a bag of salty water with structure — water is roughly 60% of your body weight.

items: You are, more than anything else, a bag of salty water with structure — water is roughly 60% of your body weight.
That water is not one big pool. It is divided into rooms (compartments), and each room has a different salt recipe.
The walls between the rooms are cell membranes, and the whole of this topic is really about one question: what gets through the wall, and what does it cost?
Everything later in physiology — nerves firing, the heart beating, the kidney making urine, a drip running into a patient — is built on these gradients.
Total body water (TBW) ≈ 60% of body weight in an average adult man, closer to 50% in an adult woman.
Muscle is wet, fat is dry. Lean tissue is about three-quarters water; fat tissue holds very little.
So the percentage tracks body composition: more fat → lower % water. That is the whole reason for the sex difference (women carry proportionally more body fat).
Babies ≈ 75% water; the elderly less — because muscle mass falls with age.
The catch to remember: the water content of lean tissue itself barely changes. What changes between people is how much lean tissue they have.
Two friends weigh the same, but one is lean and one is heavier-set — the lean one carries several litres more water, and handles a hot day or a night out far better.
A baby with diarrhoea can go from playful to critically ill in hours: they hold more water for their size and lose it faster than an adult.
This is also why drug doses and IV fluids are calculated per kilogram, and why the same amount of alcohol hits two people of equal weight very differently.

blocks.x: Think of your body as a fish tank. The fish (your cells) can only survive if the water around them stays just right — not too salty, not too fresh, not too hot or cold. Your body fluids ARE that water. Every cell you have is bathed in fluid, and life itself depends on keeping that fluid's composition almost perfectly constant.

blocks.name: Total Body Water (TBW)
blocks.def: The total amount of water in the body. Water is the single largest chemical component of the human body and is the essential medium of the body's internal environment — nothing works without it.

blocks.name: TBW as a percentage of body weight
blocks.def: Varies with age, fat, and sex: about 73% of body weight in infants, about 60% in adults, and as low as 45% in old age. Simple memory hook: babies are 'balloons of water,' the elderly are comparatively 'dried out.'

blocks.name: Why TBW declines with age
blocks.def: As we age, we gradually lose lean tissue and water content declines — this is a normal, gradual dehydration of the body's tissue composition, not a disease.

blocks.name: Why TBW correlates inversely with body fat
blocks.def: Adipose (fat) tissue is the LEAST hydrated tissue in the body — fat barely holds any water at all. So the fatter a person is, the lower their percentage of body weight that is water, even though their body may weigh more overall.

blocks.name: Sex difference in TBW
blocks.def: Water makes up about 55–60% of body weight in men but only about 45–50% in young women — because women naturally carry more body fat, and fat holds little water.

blocks.name: The constant: water in lean body mass
blocks.def: No matter your age, sex, or body fat, if you look specifically at 'lean body mass' (muscle and organs, fat excluded), it is remarkably constant at about 73% water. This is the one number that barely changes — it's the water content of 'metabolically active' tissue itself.

sections.title: Daily Water Balance — In Must Equal Out

items: The rule is boringly simple: what comes in must equal what goes out — about 2300 mL a day. Break the rule and you either swell or dry out.
In: what you drink, water hidden inside food, and metabolic water — water your cells actually manufacture while burning fuel.
Out: urine (the big one, and the only one the body can freely adjust), skin and lungs, sweat, and a little in stool.
Insensible loss = the water you lose without ever noticing — evaporating from skin and breathed out of your lungs. Sensible loss = the kind you can see and measure, like sweat and urine.
Only the kidney can really negotiate. The lungs will keep taking their cut whether you can spare it or not.
Breathe on a cold mirror and it fogs — that is insensible loss, made visible.
Dark, strong-smelling urine after a hot afternoon is the kidney clawing back water, not a sign you are ill.
In hard exercise or Kumasi afternoon heat, sweat can rise to litres per hour — far faster than thirst reacts, which is why athletes are told to drink before they feel thirsty.

blocks.x: Picture your body as a bathtub with the drain and the tap running at the exact same rate, all day, every day. That's water balance: in a steady state, water intake equals water loss, and the total amount barely budges — TBW is estimated to vary by less than 1% over 24 hours.
▶️Water Balance in the BodyVideo · Non Stop Neurone

blocks.name: Water input sources (roughly 2300 ml/day)
blocks.def: Water enters the body from three sources: drinking (about 1500 ml/day), eating (about 500 ml/day — food itself contains water), and the metabolism of food (about 400 ml/day, water produced as a byproduct of breaking down nutrients).

blocks.name: Factors affecting water intake
blocks.def: How much water a person drinks and needs depends on climate (hot climates demand more), habits, and level of physical activity.

blocks.name: Insensible water loss
blocks.def: Water lost from the body that you don't notice or control — lost continuously through the lungs (as water vapor in exhaled breath) and through the skin (evaporation), even without visibly sweating.

blocks.name: Sensible water loss
blocks.def: Water loss you DO notice and that varies with need: sweating, urine, and feces.

blocks.name: Normal daily water output breakdown
blocks.def: Roughly: skin 350 ml, lungs 350 ml, sweat 100 ml, feces 100 ml, urine 1400 ml — totaling about 2300 ml, matching intake exactly.

blocks.name: Water balance during prolonged heavy exercise
blocks.def: Sweat losses can rocket from about 100 ml/day up to 5000 ml/day, and insensible lung loss also rises (faster breathing) — total output can hit 6600 ml/day. This is why athletes must deliberately increase fluid intake during intense, prolonged exercise, or the 'in equals out' balance breaks and dehydration sets in.

sections.title: Body Fluid Compartments — Where the Water Lives

items: Two main rooms: inside the cells (ICF) ≈ two-thirds of body water, and outside the cells (ECF) ≈ one-third.
The ECF is itself split into plasma (water inside blood vessels) and interstitial fluid (water in the gaps bathing the cells).
The recipes differ sharply: inside cells is a potassium (K⁺) world; outside cells is a sodium (Na⁺) and chloride (Cl⁻) world.
Transcellular fluid is the small specialist set — cerebrospinal fluid, joint fluid, digestive juices, fluid in the eye.
Nothing about this arrangement is passive: the difference is maintained continuously by pumps burning ATP. Stop paying, and the difference disappears.
A heavily salted meal leaves you thirsty and puffy the next morning — extra Na⁺ pulled water into the ECF, and the swelling shows in the interstitial fluid around your eyes and fingers.
When someone is on a drip, the fluid enters the plasma first, then spreads outward — which is precisely why which fluid a patient is given matters so much.

blocks.x: Imagine your body's water divided between two giant rooms, separated by a wall (the cell membrane). Two-thirds of all your water is INSIDE that wall (inside cells), and one-third is OUTSIDE it (surrounding the cells and in the blood). This 2:1 split is one of the most important ratios in physiology — memorize it as 'inside wins 2 to 1.'
▶️Body Fluid Compartments (ICF, ECF & Transcellular Fluids)Video · Non Stop Neurone

blocks.cap: How Total Body Water splits between ICF, ECF, and the ECF subcompartments.

blocks.name: <term d="The fluid inside the body's cells — the largest fluid compartment in the body.">Intracellular Fluid</term> (ICF)
blocks.def: The fluid found INSIDE the cells of the body. It comprises about 2/3 of Total Body Water and makes up about 40% of body weight. Think: ICF = 'In Cells, Full 2/3.'

blocks.name: ICF ionic composition
blocks.def: High in potassium (K+), magnesium, phosphate, organic anions, and proteins; LOW in sodium, bicarbonate, and chloride. Memory hook: inside the cell, Potassium is King (K for both).

blocks.name: <term d="All the body fluid sitting outside the cells, including blood plasma and the fluid bathing tissues.">Extracellular Fluid</term> (ECF)
blocks.def: The fluid found OUTSIDE the cells. It comprises the remaining 1/3 of Total Body Water, making up about 20% of body weight.

blocks.name: ECF ionic composition
blocks.def: Low in potassium and magnesium; HIGH in sodium, chloride, and bicarbonate — essentially the mirror opposite of ICF. Memory hook: outside the cell, Sodium rules the Sea (both S).

blocks.name: <term d="The fluid sitting in the spaces between cells, delivering supplies and carrying waste away.">Interstitial Fluid</term> (ISF)
blocks.def: The subcompartment of ECF that directly surrounds the cells (but is not inside a vessel). It does not circulate, makes up about 3/4 of the ECF, and is the ONLY fluid compartment that actually declines with age.

blocks.name: <term d="The straw-coloured liquid part of blood that carries the cells, proteins, nutrients and wastes.">Plasma</term>
blocks.def: The fluid subcompartment of ECF that circulates as part of the blood. It makes up about 1/4 of the ECF. Unlike interstitial fluid, plasma is constantly moving because it's pumped by the heart.

blocks.name: Transcellular fluid
blocks.def: A small, specialized subset of ECF (about 0.5–2 liters total) contained within epithelial-lined spaces outside the normal compartments — includes cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), GI tract fluids, aqueous humor of the eye, joint fluid, and pericardial/peritoneal fluids. Small in volume but functionally very important (e.g., CSF cushions the brain).

blocks.name: The cell membrane's role in fluid compartments
blocks.def: The cell membrane is the physical wall that separates ICF from ECF, and it is because this wall allows water through freely (but tightly controls ions) that the ICF and ECF can have dramatically different ion compositions while staying in water balance with each other.

sections.title: What Water Actually Does for You

items: Solvent — nearly every reaction in you happens dissolved in water. No water, no chemistry.
Transport — it carries oxygen, nutrients, hormones and waste from place to place.
Temperature control — water absorbs a lot of heat for a small rise in temperature, so it stops you cooking from the inside; sweating then dumps that heat.
Lubrication and cushioning — joint fluid, tears, the fluid around the brain and around a fetus.
Reactant — it takes part in reactions itself, splitting molecules during digestion.

blocks.name: Functions of water in the body
blocks.def: Water transports nutrients and oxygen into cells, moisturizes the air in the lungs, helps with metabolism, protects vital organs (cushioning), helps organs absorb nutrients better, regulates body temperature, detoxifies the body, and protects/moisturizes joints. Simple truth: we cannot function without H2O — it isn't one job, it's the platform every other job runs on.

sections.title: Measuring Fluid Compartments — The Dilution Principle

items: You cannot pour a person out and measure them, so physiologists use a trick: add a known amount of a marker, let it spread, and see how weak it becomes.
The maths is one line: Volume = amount injected ÷ concentration after mixing. The more it gets diluted, the bigger the space it spread into.
The clever part is choosing a marker that stops where you want it to — one that stays trapped in blood vessels measures plasma; one that spreads everywhere measures total body water.
A good marker must mix evenly, stay put long enough to measure, not be destroyed or rapidly excreted, and not be toxic.
Some compartments are measured by subtraction, because no marker goes only there: ICF = TBW − ECF, and interstitial = ECF − plasma.
It is exactly what you do when you stir one sachet of squash into an unknown bucket of water: taste how strong it is and you know how big the bucket was.
Same logic as a drop of dye in a swimming pool versus in a cup — the fainter the colour, the larger the volume.

blocks.x: You can't just stick a ruler into someone's bloodstream to measure fluid volume. Instead, scientists use a clever trick called the dilution principle: put a KNOWN amount of a marker substance into a fluid space, let it spread out evenly, then measure how DILUTE it became — and from that, calculate the volume it spread into.

blocks.name: Dilution principle — the core idea
blocks.def: If you know exactly how much of a substance you added, and you measure its final concentration after it has spread evenly through a fluid space, you can calculate the volume of that space: Volume = Amount added ÷ Final concentration.

blocks.name: Dilution principle worked example
blocks.def: If 25 mg of glucose is added to an unknown volume of water and the final concentration is 0.05 mg/ml, then Volume = 25 mg ÷ 0.05 mg/ml = 500 ml. This is the exact logic used to measure real body fluid compartments.

blocks.name: Required characteristics of a good marker substance
blocks.def: A marker used to measure a fluid compartment must be: water soluble, measurable, must remain in the compartment being measured (not leak elsewhere), must not alter water distribution, must not be toxic, must not be secreted by the body, must remain chemically unchanged in the body, and any amount excreted or degraded must be measurable (so it can be corrected for).

blocks.name: Measuring Total Body Water (TBW)
blocks.def: Measured using heavy water — deuterium oxide or tritiated water (tritium oxide) — substances that mix freely with ALL body water, both inside and outside cells.

blocks.name: Measuring ECF volume
blocks.def: Measured using markers that spread through extracellular fluid but cannot cross into cells: inulin, mannitol, sucrose, or radioactive isotopes (e.g., 82Br, 35SO4, chloride isotopes).

blocks.name: Measuring plasma volume
blocks.def: Measured using markers that stay within blood vessels: radioiodinated human serum albumin (RISA) or Evans blue dye.

blocks.name: Measuring interstitial fluid volume
blocks.def: Cannot be measured directly. Instead it is calculated as the DIFFERENCE: Interstitial volume = ECF volume − Plasma volume.

blocks.name: Measuring ICF volume
blocks.def: Cannot be measured directly either. It is calculated by subtraction: ICF volume = TBW − ECF volume.

blocks.name: Blood volume
blocks.def: Makes up about 6–8% of body weight in a healthy adult (around 5 liters). Unlike the other compartments, blood volume contains BOTH ECF (plasma) and ICF (inside red blood cells) at once.

blocks.name: Measuring blood volume
blocks.def: Measured using radioactive isotopes (32P, 55Fe/59Fe, 51Cr) that tag red blood cells, injected intravenously, with blood volume determined by the dilution principle. Alternatively, blood volume can be calculated from plasma volume if the hematocrit (the fraction of blood volume made of red cells) is known.

blocks.name: Blood volume calculation example
blocks.def: If plasma volume is 3 liters and the hematocrit is 0.40 (40% of blood is red cells, 60% is plasma), then total blood volume = plasma volume ÷ (1 − hematocrit) = 3 ÷ 0.60 = 5 liters.

sections.title: The Cell Membrane — The Body's Smartest Wall

items: The membrane is not a brick wall — it is a thin, oily, self-healing film two molecules thick, with proteins floating in it like boats.
Phospholipids build it because each one is two-faced: a water-loving head and water-hating tails. Drop them in water and they spontaneously arrange tails-inward — the bilayer builds itself.
That oily middle decides everything: fat-soluble things (oxygen, CO₂, steroid hormones) slip straight through; water-soluble things (ions, glucose) cannot and need a door.
Cholesterol is the thermostat — it stops the membrane going too stiff when cold or too runny when warm.
Proteins are the machinery: channels and carriers (doors), pumps (powered doors), receptors (antennae), enzymes and anchors.
Carbohydrates on the outer face (the glycocalyx) are the name badge — how cells recognise each other, and how your blood group is defined.
Oil poured on water spreads and re-seals itself when you poke it — the same physics that lets a membrane close over instantly.
Why soap cleans grease and also destroys germs: it dissolves the oily membrane.
Steroid creams work through the skin's cells easily because steroids are fat-soluble and walk straight through membranes — while insulin has to be injected and must knock at a surface receptor.

blocks.x: If body fluids are the water in the fish tank, the cell membrane is the glass wall of each individual fish — thin, flexible, but incredibly selective about what it lets through. It is not a passive barrier; it's an active gatekeeper.

blocks.cap: The phospholipid bilayer, with cholesterol and integral/peripheral proteins.

blocks.name: Plasma membrane (cell membrane)
blocks.def: Also called the plasmalemma or 'phospholipid bilayer' — a semipermeable lipid bilayer that encloses the contents of a cell. It serves as the attachment point for the intracellular cytoskeleton, acts as a highly selective barrier controlling what enters/exits, detects signals, enables cell-to-cell communication, helps establish cell identity, and protects the cell's interior from the extracellular environment.

blocks.name: Physical dimensions of the plasma membrane
blocks.def: A thin, pliable, elastic structure, only 7.5–10 nanometers thick — roughly 10,000 times thinner than a sheet of paper, yet strong enough to hold an entire cell together.

blocks.name: Three principal components of the plasma membrane
blocks.def: Lipids, proteins, and carbohydrates — the relative amounts of each depend on the membrane's specific location and role in the body (a nerve membrane and a muscle membrane are not identical).

blocks.name: Three major classes of membrane lipids
blocks.def: Phospholipids, cholesterol, and glycolipids. Different membranes mix these three in different ratios depending on function.

blocks.name: Phospholipids
blocks.def: The main structural components of the lipid bilayer. Each phospholipid is a small molecule with a hydrophilic ('water-loving') phosphate head and a hydrophobic ('water-fearing') fatty acid tail — like a matchstick with a water-loving head and a water-hating tail.

blocks.name: How the phospholipid bilayer forms
blocks.def: The hydrophobic tails of phospholipids align next to each other, away from water, forming a bilayer with the hydrophilic heads pointing outward on both sides (facing the watery ICF and ECF). The whole structure is held together by non-covalent (weak) interactions of the tails, which is why the membrane is fluid, not rigid — think of it as a sea of oil sandwiched between two layers of water-friendly heads.

blocks.name: Fluid mosaic nature of the membrane
blocks.def: The membrane is not fixed rigidly in place — it behaves like a fluid, with components able to drift sideways. The right ratio of saturated to unsaturated fatty acids keeps the membrane appropriately fluid at body temperature.

blocks.name: Membrane impermeability to water-soluble substances
blocks.def: The lipid bilayer itself is impenetrable to water-soluble molecules and ions — this is exactly why cells need specialized transport proteins (channels and carriers) to let such substances in and out.

blocks.name: Cholesterol's role in the membrane
blocks.def: A steroid lipid that sits between phospholipid molecules. It reduces membrane fluidity (by limiting phospholipid movement), provides mechanical stability, decreases permeability to small water-soluble molecules, yet paradoxically also lowers the temperature at which the membrane would solidify — helping keep it fluid across a range of temperatures. Cholesterol is a stabilizer and fluidity-buffer at once.

items: The lipids you just read about decide what cannot cross. The proteins coming next decide what can.
Integral proteins go right through the membrane — these become the channels, carriers, pumps and receptors.
Peripheral proteins sit on one surface only — anchors, enzymes and structural supports.

blocks.name: Integral membrane proteins
blocks.def: Proteins attached to the lipid bilayer by hydrophobic portions. Transmembrane proteins span the ENTIRE thickness of the membrane, with hydrophilic ends exposed on both the inside and outside. Monotopic proteins are embedded into only ONE side of the membrane.

blocks.name: Peripheral membrane proteins
blocks.def: Proteins that are NOT embedded in the lipid bilayer at all — they sit on the membrane surface, held by ionic and hydrogen-bond interactions, and can be stripped off with high salt or alkaline solutions.

blocks.name: Functions of membrane proteins
blocks.def: Membrane proteins act as channels, carrier proteins, receptors, enzymes, cell adhesion molecules (CAMs), gap junctions, desmosomes, tight junctions, antigens, sites of surface recognition, and points of cytoskeleton contact — proteins do almost all of the membrane's 'active' jobs.

items: Carbohydrates appear on the outer face only, which is itself the point: they face the world.
Treat this group as the cell's name badge — recognition, immune identity, cell-to-cell sticking.
This is where your blood group physically lives (Topic 08).

blocks.name: Membrane carbohydrates and the glycocalyx
blocks.def: Carbohydrates make up about 3% of membrane weight, usually as short branched sugar chains (fewer than 15 units). Most are bonded to proteins (forming glycoproteins) or to lipids (forming glycolipids), creating a loose sugary coat called the glycocalyx that faces outward, away from the cytoplasm.

blocks.name: Functions of membrane carbohydrates
blocks.def: They act as receptors, cell adhesion molecules, and sites of surface recognition, and may participate in immune reactions — essentially, the glycocalyx is the cell's 'ID badge' that other cells and immune cells read.

blocks.name: Membrane asymmetry
blocks.def: The cell membrane has a different composition on one side than the other. Example: in an intestinal epithelial cell, the apical surface (facing the gut) selectively absorbs nutrients and has specific transport proteins; the lateral surface has junction proteins for cell-to-cell communication; the basal surface anchors to the extracellular matrix and exchanges substances with the blood. One membrane, three different jobs depending on which face you're looking at.

sections.title: Membrane Transport — Getting Things In and Out

items: Every transport method answers just two questions: does it need a helper protein? and does it cost energy?
Downhill, no help — simple diffusion. Things spread from crowded to less crowded until evened out. Free of charge.

Downhill, with help — facilitated diffusion. Channels and carriers let ions and glucose through. Still free, but because there is a fixed number of doors it can saturate — like a queue at limited turnstiles.
Uphill, paying with ATP — primary active transport. The star is the Na⁺/K⁺ pump: 3 Na⁺ out, 2 K⁺ in, every cycle, forever.
Uphill, paying indirectly — secondary active transport. One substance rides in on the sodium gradient the pump already built, like freewheeling downhill on someone else's road.
Diffusion is fast over microscopic distances and hopelessly slow over long ones — which is exactly why you need a circulation rather than just waiting for oxygen to spread.
Perfume crossing a room, or tea colouring hot water: simple diffusion, no energy required, driven only by crowding.
A crowd streaming out of a stadium gate (down a gradient) versus climbing an escalator (energy paid): diffusion versus active transport.
The Na⁺/K⁺ pump quietly consumes a large share of your resting calories — a real part of what you eat each day is spent just holding the gradient still.

blocks.x: Every cell constantly needs to bring things in (nutrients, oxygen) and push things out (waste, secretions). Membrane transport is the umbrella term for every mechanism the cell uses to move solutes across its border. There are really just two big strategies: let it happen on its own (passive/<term d="Movement of particles from an area where they are crowded to where they are sparse, until evenly spread.">diffusion</term>) or spend energy to force it (active transport).

blocks.cap: Four ways substances cross the membrane, and whether each needs energy.

blocks.name: Membrane transport (overview)
blocks.def: The collection of mechanisms that regulate movement of solutes across a cell membrane. Cell membranes are differentially (semi-) permeable — they let some things through freely and block others.

blocks.name: What determines whether a particle can cross
blocks.def: Two properties: the particle's relative solubility in lipid (fat-soluble things cross easily), and the particle's size (small things cross more easily than large ones).

blocks.name: Two basic transport processes
blocks.def: Diffusion (passive transport) and active transport — the fundamental split is whether the cell spends energy (active) or not (passive).

blocks.name: Diffusion (general definition)
blocks.def: The random thermal motion of molecules resulting in a net flux toward regions of LOWER concentration, until equilibrium is reached. No energy is spent — molecules just naturally spread out, like a drop of ink spreading through water.

blocks.name: Time required for diffusion
blocks.def: Proportional to the SQUARE of the diffusion distance — meaning diffusion is fast over short distances but becomes dramatically, disproportionately slower over longer distances. This is exactly why cells are small and why the body needs a circulatory system for long-distance transport rather than relying on diffusion alone.

blocks.name: Simple diffusion
blocks.def: A substance passes directly through the membrane WITHOUT the help of any protein. Lipid-soluble (non-polar) substances cross membranes far more readily than water-soluble substances; membranes are essentially impermeable to large water-soluble molecules. Movement is always from higher to lower concentration.

blocks.name: Fick's First Law of Diffusion
blocks.def: States that diffusive flux across a membrane is directly proportional to the concentration difference across the membrane, the surface area of the membrane, and the diffusion coefficient — and inversely proportional to the membrane's thickness. In plain terms: bigger concentration gap, bigger surface, thinner membrane = faster diffusion.

blocks.name: Ionic diffusion
blocks.def: Ions are relatively lipid-insoluble, so they diffuse via protein channels rather than directly through the lipid. These channel proteins form hydrophilic pores across the bilayer, may be selectively permeable to specific substances, and can be opened or closed by 'gates.'

blocks.name: Types of gated ion channels
blocks.def: Voltage-gated (open/close in response to membrane voltage changes), <term d="Any molecule that binds to a receptor to deliver a signal.">ligand</term> (chemical)-gated (open/close when a specific chemical binds), and mechanically-gated (open/close in response to physical force/stretch).

blocks.name: What drives ionic movement
blocks.def: Ionic diffusion is affected by BOTH the concentration gradient and the ion's electrical charge — the net transmembrane flux of an ion is proportional to the combined effect of these electrical and chemical (concentration) gradients together, called the electrochemical gradient.

blocks.title: Next up — downhill, but needs a door

items: Everything so far was unassisted. From here a protein is involved.
Still no ATP — the particle is still moving downhill; the protein just provides a route through the oily layer.
Because doors are limited in number, this group can saturate — the key difference from simple diffusion.

blocks.name: Facilitated diffusion
blocks.def: Like simple diffusion, net flux is still DOWN the electrochemical gradient (no energy needed) — but it requires a membrane carrier protein. Binding of the transported molecule to the carrier causes a conformational (shape) change in the protein, which shuttles the molecule across. Classic examples: glucose and amino acid transport.

blocks.name: Characteristics of facilitated diffusion / carrier-mediated transport
blocks.def: More rapid than simple diffusion; shows saturation (a maximum transport rate once all carriers are busy); shows specificity (though not absolute — structurally related molecules can compete for the same carrier); and can be inhibited by substances that are NOT even structurally related to what's being transported (e.g., the Na-K-ATPase pump is inhibited by the drug digoxin).

blocks.title: Next up — uphill, and someone must pay

items: The switch here is direction: these move substances against their gradient.
Primary = pays directly with ATP (the Na⁺/K⁺ pump).
Secondary = pays indirectly, riding the sodium gradient the pump already built.
One-line test: if it goes uphill, energy is being spent somewhere — the only question is by whom.

blocks.name: Active transport (general definition)
blocks.def: Substances are moved AGAINST their electrochemical gradient (uphill, from low to high concentration) — this requires both a carrier protein AND energy. Like facilitated diffusion, it shows carrier-mediated characteristics (saturation, specificity, competition).

blocks.x: ▶️Primary vs Secondary Active TransportVideo · Non Stop Neurone

blocks.name: Primary active transport
blocks.def: Uses metabolic energy directly, in the form of ATP. Classic examples: Na+/K+-ATPase, Ca2+-ATPase, H+/K+-ATPase — each of these pumps literally burns ATP to move ions uphill.

blocks.name: Secondary active transport
blocks.def: A form of active transport where a transporter couples the DOWNHILL movement of one ion (usually Na+, moving down its electrochemical gradient) to the UPHILL movement of another molecule against its gradient. It uses metabolic energy only indirectly — driven by the energy already stored in an ion gradient (which was itself set up by primary active transport), rather than by directly hydrolyzing ATP. Examples: co-transport of Na+ with glucose, or Na+ with amino acids.

blocks.title: Next up — naming carriers by direction

items: These three names describe nothing but how many passengers, and which way.
Uniport = one substance, one direction.
Symport = two substances, same direction. Antiport = two substances, opposite directions.
Hook: sym = same; anti = against.

blocks.name: Uniport transporters
blocks.def: Membrane transport proteins that move just ONE kind of solute across the lipid bilayer.

blocks.name: Cotransport systems
blocks.def: Transporters that move TWO OR MORE different solutes across the membrane simultaneously; associated with secondary active transport. There are two types: symport and antiport.

blocks.name: Symport
blocks.def: A cotransport system where the solutes are moved in the SAME direction across the membrane.

blocks.name: Antiport
blocks.def: A cotransport system where the solutes are moved in OPPOSITE directions across the membrane.

blocks.title: Next up — for cargo too big for any door

items: Proteins and bacteria cannot fit through a channel, so the membrane wraps around them instead.
Endocytosis = in; exocytosis = out. Both cost energy.
This is how a white cell swallows bacteria (Topic 08) and how a neuron releases transmitter (Topic 07).

blocks.name: Vesicular transport (overview)
blocks.def: Movement of macromolecules within membrane-bound vesicles across the cell membrane — used for cargo too large to fit through channels or carriers. The two main types are endocytosis and exocytosis.

blocks.name: Endocytosis
blocks.def: The uptake of macromolecules into the cell. The material to be internalized is surrounded by an area of plasma membrane, which then buds off inward to form a vesicle. The molecule responsible for pinching off the vesicle is called dynamin. Endocytosis requires metabolic energy.

blocks.name: Three types of endocytosis
blocks.def: Phagocytosis ('cell eating' — uptake of large particles), pinocytosis ('cell drinking' — uptake of small molecules suspended in ECF), and receptor-mediated endocytosis (highly selective uptake via specific receptors, e.g., how mammalian cells take up cholesterol).

blocks.name: Exocytosis
blocks.def: The process by which materials packaged inside vesicles are secreted OUT of the cell, when the vesicle membrane fuses with the plasma membrane. Requires energy AND calcium (Ca2+). Critical for expelling waste and for secreting products like digestive enzymes, neurotransmitters, and hormones.

blocks.name: Caveolae
blocks.def: Small pouch-like invaginations of the plasma membrane, important for signal transduction and macromolecule uptake. Their formation depends on the protein caveolin — without caveolin, no caveolae exist. Uptake of molecules by caveolae specifically is termed potocytosis.

blocks.name: <term d="Movement of water across a membrane, from where dissolved particles are few toward where they are many.">Osmosis</term>
blocks.def: The passive diffusion of WATER (not solutes) across a semipermeable membrane, from a region of LOW solute concentration to a region of HIGH solute concentration — equivalently, water moves from where water concentration is high to where it is low. Presence of solute lowers the 'chemical potential' of water, and osmosis generates a hydrostatic ('water-stopping') pressure.

blocks.title: Next up — water plays by its own rules

items: Everything above was about solutes moving. This last group is about water moving.
Water follows solute: it moves toward wherever things are more concentrated.
Aquaporins are dedicated water channels; filtration is water pushed by pressure rather than pulled by concentration.

blocks.name: Osmotic pressure
blocks.def: The hydrostatic pressure that would need to be applied to exactly stop the net flow of water by osmosis. If you raise the pressure on the receiving side to match the osmotic pressure, water movement stops entirely. Osmotic pressure depends on the NUMBER of particles in solution, not their identity.

blocks.name: <term d="A contraction where the muscle shortens while the load on it stays the same.">Isotonic</term>, <term d="A solution more concentrated than the cell, so water leaves the cell and it shrinks.">hypertonic</term>, <term d="A solution more dilute than the cell, so water enters the cell and it swells.">hypotonic</term> solutions
blocks.def: If two solutions have EQUAL osmotic pressure, they are isotonic to each other. If solution A has GREATER osmotic pressure than solution B, A is hypertonic to B. If A has LESS osmotic pressure than B, A is hypotonic to B.

blocks.name: Aquaporins
blocks.def: Transmembrane proteins containing dedicated water channels that let water diffuse rapidly across cell membranes — without aquaporins, water would still cross via the lipid bilayer, but far more slowly.

blocks.name: Filtration
blocks.def: The process by which fluid is forced through a membrane or barrier because of a PRESSURE difference across it (not a concentration difference, unlike diffusion). The amount of fluid filtered is proportional to the pressure difference, the surface area of the membrane, and the membrane's permeability.

items: 60–40–20: total body water ≈ 60% of body weight, ICF ≈ 40%, ECF ≈ 20%.
ECF splits 15 / 5: about 15% interstitial, 5% plasma.
'Bananas live inside': K⁺ (bananas) is the intracellular ion; Na⁺ and Cl⁻ (table salt) live outside.
Fat is dry, muscle is wet — that one line explains every age and sex difference in body water.
Volume = amount ÷ concentration — the whole dilution principle in four symbols.

blocks.title: Cleared up — the confusions that cost marks

items: Facilitated diffusion is not active transport. It uses a protein but no ATP. Using a helper ≠ spending energy — this is the single commonest mistake in this topic.
Diffusion moves solute; osmosis moves water. Same underlying idea, opposite thing moving.
Primary vs secondary active transport: both go uphill. Primary pays ATP directly; secondary borrows a gradient someone else paid for.
'Semi-permeable' does not mean leaky. The membrane is highly selective, not partially broken.
→ Homeostasis (Topic 02): the 'internal environment' every control system defends is the ECF you just met. Keeping it stable is what homeostasis actually means.
→ Excitable Tissues (Topic 03): the Na⁺/K⁺ pump is charging a battery. Nerve and muscle signals are that stored charge being spent — this topic builds the battery, the next one uses it.
→ Blood & CVS (Topic 08): plasma is simply the ECF that lives inside blood vessels, and blood volume depends directly on how the water is shared out.
The one-line summary: gradients are expensive to build and useful to spend — the rest of physiology is a story about spending them wisely.

lines: Total body water is about 60% of body weight: 40% inside cells, 20% outside — and of that outside fraction, roughly 15% interstitial and 5% plasma.
Potassium is the dominant intracellular cation and sodium the dominant extracellular one; the Na<sup>+</sup>/K<sup>+</sup> pump is what keeps that difference standing.
A quick estimate of plasma osmolarity, normally about 285–295 mOsm/L, because sodium and its anions carry most of the osmotic load.
Capillary hydrostatic and interstitial oncotic push fluid out; plasma oncotic and interstitial hydrostatic pull it back — oedema is that balance losing.
